newsitem.title: UK: Blue Circle seals UK "job security" pacts.
newsitem.headline: Blue Circle seals UK "job security" pacts.

text.p: Building materials group Blue Circle Plc, Britain's biggest cement producer, said on Monday it had sealed two ground-breaking long-term labour pacts with trade unions that would bring both productivity gains and job security to a sector overshadowed by losses and cutbacks for years.
The deals are in two parts and cover cement distribution drivers and process, craft and staff workers respectively. Senior union and company officials gave them a warm welcome.
"The basis is a security from employment' agreement," cement division personnel director Ross Dunn told Reuters in a telephone interview, adding, "We have to take the fear away".

In the case of the company's drivers, with whom Blue Circle has signed a five-year package, Dunn said that a renewed focus on strengthening the company's core fleet of trucks meant that, on balance, he did not expect any change in numbers over time.

The parallel deal with 2,000 factory workers, due to be ratified this week, also contains a commitment to improve the performance of the business, twinned with a pledge that any cuts in job numbers would be done by through voluntary redundancies.
Blue Circle and the unions said they hoped this part would be a rolling three-year deal that they would be able to extend.
Alan Black, national secretary of large GMB union, told Reuters he throught the drivers' deal was a first. "It was very much ground-breaking," he said.
Black added that, from a trade union point of view, he hoped similar deals would be repeated across the British building materials and construction sector.

"The period since 1990 has been the most difficult period that I remember," added Black, who has been active in the industry for 23 years. The sector has seen tens of thousands of layoffs and job losses as firms struggle to balance profits and market share amid downward pressures on both volumes and prices.

Blue Circle's efforts to offset the impact of dwindling UK cement volumes has so far involved restructuring operations, in a bid to become Europe's most cost-efficient producer, and boosting its overseas businesses.
Last September, it reported interim pretax profits up nearly 12 percent at 116.3 million pounds ($196 million).
